# Cluster headache

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Neurology > Headaches and facial pain > Cluster headache*

[Original Article Link](/library/Ri0lrf)

---

## Summary

Cluster <u>headache</u> (CH) is a type of <u>primary headache</u> that mostly affects adult men. Patients present with recurrent attacks of agonizing, strictly unilateral <u>headaches</u> in the periorbital and forehead region (areas innervated by the <u>trigeminal nerve</u>) that last from fifteen minutes up to three hours. These attacks are associated with <u>ipsilateral</u> symptoms of increased <u>cranial</u> autonomic activity, e.g., <u>lacrimation</u>, <u>conjunctival injection</u>, <u>rhinorrhea</u>, or <u>partial Horner syndrome</u>. Cluster <u>headaches</u> tend to occur in episodic patterns (called <u>cluster periods</u> or <u>cluster bouts</u>) followed by months of remission; they are considered chronic if remission between bouts lasts less than three months. Diagnosis is based on the patient's history, in particular on the exact description and timing of the <u>headaches</u>. In patients with <u>red flag symptoms for headache</u>, <u>secondary headache</u> should be ruled out using an <u>MRI</u>. Acute episodes are treated with 100% oxygen and/or <u>triptans</u>, and <u>verapamil</u> is most commonly used as prophylaxis.

---

## Epidemiology

* Sex: : <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u> (3:1) [[1]](/library/A0bRiH)

* Peak <u>incidence</u>: 20–40 years [[2]](/library/lGYvzq)

* <u>Prevalence</u>: rare, ∼ 0.1% of general population [[1]](/library/A0bRiH)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

The etiology of cluster <u>headache</u> is not entirely understood but is thought to involve a genetic component.




* <u>Risk factor</u>: : tobacco use  [[1]](/library/A0bRiH)[[3]](/library/MabMOH)

* Triggers of cluster headache

* <u>Alcohol</u>  [[1]](/library/A0bRiH)

* <u>Histamine</u>

* Seasonal fluctuations

* <u>Nitroglycerine</u>

* Volatile substances (solvents, oil-based paint) [[4]](/library/5abiOH)

---

## Clinical features

* <u>Headache</u> characteristics

* Agonizing <u>pain</u>

* Strictly unilateral, periorbital, and/or temporal

* Quickly developing (within minutes), short, recurring attacks;   that usually occur in a cyclical pattern (“<u>cluster periods</u>”) 

* May become chronic (less common), with interruptions of less than three months between <u>cluster bouts</u> [[2]](/library/lGYvzq)

* Attacks often wake patients up during <u>sleep</u>.

* <u>Ipsilateral</u> autonomic symptoms

* <u>Conjunctival</u> injections and/or <u>lacrimation</u>

* <u>Rhinorrhea</u> and nasal congestion

* Partial Horner syndrome: <u>ptosis</u> and <u>miosis</u>, but no <u>anhidrosis</u>

* Restlessness and <u>agitation</u>





> [!TIP]
> While patients with <u>migraine headaches</u> tend to rest motionlessly in a quiet, dark room, individuals with cluster <u>headache</u> pace around restlessly in excruciating <u>pain</u>!

## Differential diagnoses

See the article on “<u>Headache</u>” for more information regarding differential diagnoses.




### Paroxysmal hemicrania




* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* Rare; the exact <u>prevalence</u> is unknown

* Equal <u>gender</u> distribution: <u>♀</u> = <u>♂</u> [[11]](/library/5obicu)

* Clinical features

* Severe unilateral attacks of periorbital <u>pain</u> that recur several times per day

* <u>Cranial</u> <u>autonomic dysfunction</u> (e.g., <u>lacrimation</u>, <u>conjunctival injection</u>)

* Attacks are generally more frequent (usually ≥ 5 per day) and shorter (2–45 min) than cluster <u>headaches</u> and may occur at any time of the day.

* Treatment: no established treatment for acute attacks

* Prevention: <u>indomethacin</u>





### Short-lasting unilateral neuralgiform <u>headache</u> attacks




* Definition: a form of <u>trigeminal</u> autonomic <u>cephalgia</u> characterized by unilateral throbbing <u>pain</u> and autonomic symptoms (i.e., <u>conjunctival injection</u> and/or tearing)

* Subtypes

* Short-lasting unilateral neuralgiform headache with conjunctival injection and tearing (<u>SUNCT</u>)

* Short-lasting unilateral neuralgiform headache attacks with cranial autonomic symptoms (<u>SUNA</u>)

* Clinical features

* Unilateral throbbing, piercing, and/or burning head <u>pain</u> with temporal, orbital, or supraorbital distribution

* Attacks are frequent

* At least 1 per day

* Last between 1 second and 10 minutes as single stabs, a series of stabs, or in a saw-<u>tooth</u> pattern

* At least one <u>cranial</u> autonomic symptom is usually present

* <u>Conjunctival injection</u> and/or <u>lacrimation</u> (tearing)

* <u>Eyelid</u> <u>edema</u>

* Facial and forehead sweating

* <u>Miosis</u> and/or <u>ptosis</u>

* Nasal congestion and/or <u>rhinorrhea</u>

* Attacks can be triggered without a <u>refractory period</u>

* Diagnosis: mainly clinical following a history of at least 20 attacks; CT or <u>MRI</u> may be used to rule out other causes (e.g., <u>tumor</u>)

* <u>SUNCT</u> is diagnosed if both <u>conjunctival injection</u> AND <u>lacrimation</u> are present <u>ipsilateral</u> to the <u>pain</u>

* <u>SUNA</u> is diagnosed if not > 1 of <u>conjunctival injection</u> or <u>lacrimation</u> occurs <u>ipsilateral</u> to the <u>pain</u>

* Treatment: no abortive treatment

* Acute attacks: IV <u>lidocaine</u> decreases the frequency of attacks.

* Prevention: <u>antiepileptic drugs</u> (e.g., <u>lamotrigine</u>, <u>topiramate</u>, or <u>gabapentin</u>)

## Treatment

### Approach [[9]](/library/mg1VDT0)[[16]](/library/8GYOaI)




* Treat acute attacks using <u>oxygen therapy</u> and/or <u>triptans</u>.

* Initiate prophylactic treatment (e.g., <u>verapamil</u>) to reduce the frequency of attacks.

* Avoid <u>cluster headache triggers</u>.

* <u>Neuromodulation therapy</u> may be considered for patients with refractory symptoms.





### Acute treatment [[1]](/library/A0bRiH)[[16]](/library/8GYOaI)[[17]](/library/vGYAaI)




* First-line

* <u>Oxygen therapy</u> with <u>F<sub>i</sub>O<sub>2</sub></u> 100%: usually the first choice if available   [[1]](/library/A0bRiH)[[9]](/library/mg1VDT0)[[16]](/library/8GYOaI)[[18]](/library/svYtYr)

* <u>Triptans</u>

* Subcutaneous <u>sumatriptan</u> DOSAGE

* Or intranasal <u>zolmitriptan</u> (<u>off label</u>) DOSAGE [[9]](/library/mg1VDT0)[[16]](/library/8GYOaI)[[17]](/library/vGYAaI)

* Second-line: if first-line treatment is insufficient or not tolerated

* Consider either: 

* Intranasal <u>sumatriptan</u> (<u>off label</u>) DOSAGE [[9]](/library/mg1VDT0)[[16]](/library/8GYOaI)

* Oral <u>zolmitriptan</u> (<u>off label</u>) DOSAGE [[16]](/library/8GYOaI)[[17]](/library/vGYAaI)

* Other options : e.g., <u>ergotamine</u>, intranasal <u>lidocaine</u>, or subcutaneous <u>octreotide</u> [[16]](/library/8GYOaI)





> [!WARNING]
> Standard <u>analgesics</u> (e.g., <u>acetaminophen</u>, <u>NSAIDs</u>, <u>opioids</u>) are not recommended because they are ineffective and may lead to <u>medication overuse headache</u> if used frequently. [[19]](/library/mabVOH)




> [!TIP]
> To improve absorption, apply nasal sprays in the nostril unaffected by congestion.




### Prophylactic treatment  [[9]](/library/mg1VDT0)[[16]](/library/8GYOaI)[[20]](/library/ZabZQH)[[21]](/library/DZ11d20)




* Prophylactic agents

* <u>Verapamil</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE : usually the first choice despite mixed evidence [[9]](/library/mg1VDT0)[[16]](/library/8GYOaI)[[21]](/library/DZ11d20)

* If <u>verapamil</u> is ineffective or not tolerated, consider either of the following :

* <u>Lithium</u>

* <u>Melatonin</u>

* Emerging therapies: e.g., galcanezumab , civamide   [[9]](/library/mg1VDT0)[[16]](/library/8GYOaI)

* May be stopped after the <u>episodic CH</u> period has ceased, or continued long-term for <u>chronic CH</u>.

* Transitional treatment options: Consider as a <u>bridge therapy</u> until prophylactic agents become effective. [[1]](/library/A0bRiH)[[9]](/library/mg1VDT0)[[16]](/library/8GYOaI)

* Suboccipital <u>steroid</u> injections

* Short-term <u>glucocorticoids</u> : e.g., <u>prednisone</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE or <u>methylprednisolone</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[9]](/library/mg1VDT0)





> [!TIP]
> Transitional therapy with shorter onset latencies may be necessary until prophylactic treatment takes effect.




### Neuromodulation [[1]](/library/A0bRiH)[[9]](/library/mg1VDT0)[[16]](/library/8GYOaI)




Neuromodulation is usually reserved for cluster <u>headache</u> refractory to multiple medical treatments.




* Noninvasive neurostimulation: noninvasive <u>vagus nerve</u> stimulation  [[9]](/library/mg1VDT0)

* Invasive neurostimulation: e.g., <u>sphenopalatine ganglion</u> stimulation  and occipital nerve stimulation  [[1]](/library/A0bRiH)[[16]](/library/8GYOaI)

* Disadvantages: uncertain benefits, potential for serious adverse effects

* Advantages: possible acute and prophylactic effects
